newsitem.title: UK: Grobbelaar denies guilt in UK soccer-rigging case.
newsitem.headline: Grobbelaar denies guilt in UK soccer-rigging case.

text.p: Former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar on Thursday denied he had ever thrown a British soccer match, saying he had been paid only for forecasting the results of games.

"Soccer is a business. You don't go onto the field to lose a game," he told a court in the southern city of Winchester where he and three co-defendants are on trial, accused of rigging matches for a Far Eastern betting syndicate.
"There is no way I have ever thrown a game," Grobbelaar said in a loud, clear voice.

The Zimbabwean goalkeeper is accused along with former Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers, ex-Wimbledon and Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim of rigging soccer games. All four deny the charges.
Grobbelaar, like Segers before him, acknowledged forecasting results of matches in return for cash from Lim.
"Did you believe in any way you were doing anything improper?" asked Grobbelaar's lawyer Rodney Klevan.
"Did it ever move beyond match forecasting?" asked Klevan.
"No, forecasting was the topic of the matter," said the keeper, who said he had been paid 250 pounds ($400) for each correct forecast that Lim used.

The case against the four men relies mainly on the evidence of former Grobbelaar business partner Chris Vincent, who said the keeper had decided to start throwing games in 1993 because Liverpool were not paying him enough.

Vincent, helped by the Sun tabloid newspaper, clandestinely filmed Grobbelaar as the keeper seemed to admit he had thrown games for large amounts of money. But Grobbelaar suggested in court he had done this deliberately to trap Vincent.

Grobbelaar, who lost 60,000 pounds ($98,000) in a safari company he and Vincent were trying to set up in Zimbabwe, denied much of what his former business partner had said and rejected the charge he had been unhappy with his Liverpool pay.
"I never asked them for extra money when signing a contract. I never squeezed them for more money," said the keeper, who won 13 medals when playing for Liverpool.

Vincent approached the Sun after the collapse of the safari park venture in July 1994. Grobbelaar said he had decided to stop putting in money after it transpired that much of his investment had disappeared.
"I asked him where the money had gone and he couldn't give me an answer. I have asked this over the last two and a half years and have never got a satisfactory answer," he said.
One of the main accusations against Grobbelaar is that he accepted 40,000 pounds ($65,270) from Fashanu in late November 1993 for rigging an away game against Newcastle.

Vincent said Grobbelaar had given him half the cash and asked him to pay off various debts. But the keeper told the court he had given Vincent the money a week earlier and told him to buy property in South Africa with it.

Asked by Klevan where the 20,000 pounds ($32,640) had come from, Grobbelaar said it was the proceeds from coaching spells abroad and after-dinner speeches. He kept the money in his sock drawer, he told the court.
